title: A drop of mercury can beat like a heart, powered by an iron nail

cover.alt: A shiny round drop of mercury sits in a shallow layer of clear liquid, with the thin tip of a nail touching its left edge.

body: In the **mercury beating heart**, a blob of mercury sits in an electrolyte such as sulfuric acid, with an oxidising agent such as potassium dichromate, and the tip of an iron nail almost touches it. A thin oxide layer forms on the mercury and lowers its surface tension, so the blob slumps and spreads until it touches the nail. That contact undoes the oxide: the iron is oxidised and the mercury is reduced back to bare metal. With the oxide gone the surface tension rises again, the blob pulls back into a rounder shape and loses contact, and the cycle repeats until the oxidising agent is used up.

slides.alt: Close-up of a drop of mercury beside a nail tip. Over and over, the drop stretches into a rounded triangle that bumps the nail, then shrinks back into a round blob.
slides.caption: A drop of mercury under a thin layer of solution, with a nail at its edge, keeps pulsing between a round blob and a flattened triangle.

steps.label: An oxide film forms on the mercury
Surface tension drops and the blob spreads
It touches the iron, which removes the oxide
The blob rounds up and pulls away

slides.prompt: The version of this demonstration known today was described by a German chemist famous for discovering which everyday substance?
slides.detail: Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge. The effect itself had first been seen in 1800 by Alessandro Volta and William Henry.

slides.heading: Where the energy comes from
slides.text: Overall, the oxidising agent is slowly oxidising the iron, with the mercury acting as a go-between. The oxidation happens only near the nail while reduction covers the whole drop, so the surface tension is uneven, and that sets the drop wobbling, much like other chemical oscillators.

slides.question: What finally makes the mercury heart stop beating?
slides.explanation: Each beat uses up some of the oxidising agent. Once it has all been reduced, no new oxide forms and the drop stays still.
